# Discrete-time models {#sec-discrete-time-models}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 1, Session 4. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd).
:::

Many epidemic data arrive in discrete intervals — daily case counts, weekly
reports — and many simulations advance in fixed steps. This chapter develops the
discrete-time SIR model in two flavours: a **deterministic function map** with
continuous state, and a **stochastic Markov chain** with integer counts. We then
show that as the step width $\delta t$ shrinks, the deterministic map converges
to the continuous ODE of @sec-foundations, tying the discrete and continuous
worlds together.

## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- write a discrete-time SIR update using the rate-to-proportion conversion;
- contrast the deterministic map with the continuous-time ODE of
  @sec-foundations, and say which of the two the map approximates;
- run a stochastic ensemble and compare its mean with the deterministic map;
- demonstrate numerically that the map converges to the ODE as $\delta t \to 0$;
- verify population conservation in both formulations.

## Model assumptions and classification

All three models share the SIR assumptions of @sec-foundations — closed,
well-mixed population, mass-action transmission, constant recovery. They differ
only in how they represent time and state:

| Model | Determinism | Time | State |
|---|---|---|---|
| Function map | Deterministic | Discrete | Continuous |
| Markov chain | Stochastic | Discrete | Discrete (integer) |
| ODE (@sec-foundations) | Deterministic | Continuous | Continuous |

The function map is the deterministic *expectation* of the Markov chain: it
moves the mean number of individuals each step, whereas the chain draws a random
integer around that mean.

## Equations

Over a step of width $\delta t$, the per-capita probabilities of infection and
recovery are obtained from the continuous rates via the Poisson conversion
introduced in @eq-p01-rate:

$$
p_I = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{\beta c I_t}{N}\,\delta t\right), \qquad
p_R = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\gamma\,\delta t\right).
$$ {#eq-ch02-probs}

The **deterministic map** moves the expected number of individuals:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{t+1} &= S_t - p_I S_t,\\
I_{t+1} &= I_t + p_I S_t - p_R I_t,\\
R_{t+1} &= R_t + p_R I_t.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch02-map}

The **stochastic chain** replaces those expectations with binomial draws:

$$
Y_t \sim \text{Binomial}(S_t, p_I), \quad
Z_t \sim \text{Binomial}(I_t, p_R), \quad
\begin{aligned}
S_{t+1} &= S_t - Y_t,\\
I_{t+1} &= I_t + Y_t - Z_t,\\
R_{t+1} &= R_t + Z_t.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch02-chain}

A $\text{Binomial}(n, p)$ counts how many of $n$ independent individuals, each
with probability $p$, make the move; here $n$ is the number of people at risk
and $p$ comes from @eq-ch02-probs. The same chain is derived at more length in
@sec-probability-and-stochastic-processes, which is optional background rather
than a prerequisite for this chapter.

As $\delta t \to 0$, $p_I \to \tfrac{\beta c I}{N}\delta t$ and
$p_R \to \gamma\,\delta t$, so the map @eq-ch02-map reduces to a forward-Euler
step of the ODE @eq-ch01-sir and converges to it.

## Julia implementation

The two kernels sit side by side so the only difference — deterministic movement
versus a binomial draw — is explicit.

```{julia}
#| label: ch02-kernels
using Distributions, StableRNGs

rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)

function sir_map_step(state, p, δt)          # deterministic, eq-ch02-map
    S, I, R = state
    infection = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S
    recovery  = rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt) * I
    return (S - infection, I + infection - recovery, R + recovery)
end

function sir_chain_step(state, p, δt, rng)   # stochastic, eq-ch02-chain
    S, I, R = state
    Y = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, S), rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt)))
    Z = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, I), rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt)))
    return (S - Y, I + Y - Z, R + Z)
end

function iterate_model(step, u0, p, δt, nsteps; extra = ())
    traj = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 3, nsteps + 1)
    traj[:, 1] .= u0
    state = Tuple(float.(u0))
    for k in 1:nsteps
        state = step(state, p, δt, extra...)
        traj[:, k + 1] .= state
    end
    return traj
end
```

We run the deterministic map and a 200-member stochastic ensemble on the
baseline scenario with $\delta t = 1$ day.

```{julia}
#| label: ch02-run
u0 = [990, 10, 0]
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
δt = 1.0
nsteps = 40
ts = 0:nsteps

map_traj = iterate_model((s, p, dt) -> sir_map_step(s, p, dt), u0, p, δt, nsteps)

nsims = 200
chain_ens = [iterate_model(sir_chain_step, u0, p, δt, nsteps; extra = (StableRNG(seed),))
             for seed in 1:nsims]
chain_I = reduce(hcat, (traj[2, :] for traj in chain_ens))
chain_mean_I = vec(sum(chain_I; dims = 2)) ./ nsims
(round(maximum(map_traj[2, :]); digits = 1), round(maximum(chain_mean_I); digits = 1))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ch02-compare
#| fig-cap: "Infectious compartment: stochastic Markov-chain realisations (thin grey), their ensemble mean (red), and the deterministic function map (dashed black). The map closely tracks the stochastic mean."
using CairoMakie

fig = Figure(size = (720, 440))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)",
          title = "Discrete-time SIR: map vs stochastic chain (δt = 1)")
for j in 1:nsims
    lines!(ax, ts, chain_I[:, j]; color = (:grey, 0.12), linewidth = 1)
end
lines!(ax, ts, chain_mean_I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "chain mean")
lines!(ax, ts, map_traj[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 3,
       label = "function map")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

### Convergence of the map to the ODE

As $\delta t \to 0$ the deterministic map should approach the continuous-time
ODE solution. We compare the map at the fixed horizon $t = 40$ against a
high-accuracy `Tsit5` reference across a sequence of shrinking steps.

```{julia}
#| label: ch02-convergence
using OrdinaryDiffEq

function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I; du[3] = p.γ * I
    return nothing
end

tmax = 40.0
ode_ref = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, float.(u0), (0.0, tmax), p), Tsit5();
                reltol = 1e-12, abstol = 1e-12, save_everystep = false).u[end]

δts = [tmax / 2^k for k in 5:13]
map_errors = map(δts) do dt
    n = round(Int, tmax / dt)
    traj = iterate_model((s, p, d) -> sir_map_step(s, p, d), u0, p, dt, n)
    maximum(abs.(traj[:, end] .- ode_ref))
end
[(round(dt; sigdigits = 3), round(err; sigdigits = 3)) for (dt, err) in zip(δts, map_errors)]
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ch02-convergence
#| fig-cap: "Error of the deterministic map at $t=40$ relative to the ODE solution, versus step size (log–log). The points parallel the slope-1 guide, confirming first-order convergence of the map to the ODE."
fig2 = Figure(size = (640, 420))
ax2 = Axis(fig2[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10,
           xlabel = "step size δt", ylabel = "‖map − ODE‖ at t = 40",
           title = "Map → ODE convergence")
scatter!(ax2, δts, map_errors; markersize = 12, color = :steelblue, label = "measured")
guide = map_errors[1] .* (δts ./ δts[1])
lines!(ax2, δts, guide; linestyle = :dash, color = :black, label = "slope 1")
axislegend(ax2; position = :rb)
fig2
```

## Validation

**Conservation.** Both the deterministic map and every stochastic realisation
must keep the population at $N = 1000$:

```{julia}
#| label: ch02-check-conservation
map_ok   = all(k -> isapprox(sum(map_traj[:, k]), 1000.0; atol = 1e-8), 1:nsteps+1)
chain_ok = all(traj -> all(k -> sum(traj[:, k]) == 1000, 1:nsteps+1), chain_ens)
(map_ok, chain_ok)
```

**Convergence.** The empirical order of the map-to-ODE error should be close to
1. First order means the error falls in proportion to the step: halve $\delta t$
and the error halves. The same result is derived for the forward-Euler method in
@sec-calculus-and-numerical-methods, which is optional background rather than a
prerequisite for this chapter:

```{julia}
#| label: ch02-check-order
orders = [log2(map_errors[k] / map_errors[k+1]) for k in 1:length(map_errors)-1]
mean_order = sum(orders) / length(orders)
(round(mean_order; digits = 3), isapprox(mean_order, 1.0; atol = 0.1))
```

Both cells confirm the expected behaviour: population is conserved in every
trajectory, and the map converges to the ODE at first order.

## Interpretation and limitations

The three models form a coherent family. The Markov chain is the most faithful:
it produces integer counts, allows an epidemic to fade out by chance, and shows
run-to-run variability that shrinks as the population grows. The deterministic
map is its mean-field shadow — cheap and smooth, but blind to extinction and
fluctuations. Both are only *approximations* to the continuous process, exact
only as $\delta t \to 0$; at $\delta t = 1$ day the discretisation error is
visible but modest. A subtle limitation of the binomial construction is that it
processes all infections and recoveries within a step simultaneously, so an
individual cannot become infected *and* recover in the same step — an artefact
that vanishes as the step shrinks. The exact event-driven treatment is the
subject of the continuous-time Markov chain chapter. See the
[Distributions.jl documentation](https://juliastats.org/Distributions.jl/stable/)
and the [SciML FunctionMap solver](https://docs.sciml.ai/OrdinaryDiffEq/stable/)
for the corresponding library tools.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#ch02-ex1}

Run the stochastic chain ensemble at $\delta t = 1$ and again at $\delta t = 0.25$
(with the horizon fixed at 40 days). Compare the ensemble-mean infectious peak
against the deterministic map at each step size, and explain which discretisation
sits closer to the ODE reference and why.

### Exercise 2 {#ch02-ex2}

Compute, from the 200-member ensemble, the probability that the epidemic goes
extinct (reaches $I = 0$) before day 40 for the baseline $R_0 = 2$. Then lower
the contact rate to $c = 6$ and recompute. Explain the change in terms of the
reproduction number and of demographic stochasticity, the chance variation that
comes from moving whole individuals rather than expected fractions, which the
deterministic map cannot capture.
